claim: claims that the 1st Defendant has repudiated the agreement and is seeking a reduction in price due to the 1st Defendant's alleged breach of the agreement
requested_remedy: claims that the 1st Defendant has repudiated the agreement and is seeking a reduction in price due to the 1st Defendant's alleged breach of the agreement
parties: Plaintiff: KAM KEE (HOLDINGS) LIMITED
Defendant: RICHEON COMPANY LIMITED and JOY WIN LIMITED

facts.F1: The Plaintiff and the 1st Defendant entered into a written agreement on 16 August 1997 for the sale and purchase of a shop at the Ground Floor of Pak Cheung Building in Mongkok, Kowloon for $22,800,000.00, subject to and with the benefit of an existing tenancy yielding $75,000.00 per month rental for a term of two years to expire on 22 August 1999.
facts.F2: By the end of 1997, the property market had fallen and the Plaintiff raised and maintained a number of requisitions or queries on title.
facts.F3: The tenant under the tenancy quitted the Property on 4 February 1998 and the Plaintiff charged the 1st Defendant with re-taking possession of the Property without leaving the Plaintiff the right to hold the tenant liable under the tenancy.
facts.F4: The 1st Defendant received the keys to a padlock for locking the roller shutter, a signed note from the tenant stating that he quits, and a copy of the Prohibition Order on 4 February 1998.
facts.F5: The 1st Defendant replaced the roller shutter complained of by a new one which does not protrude outside the entrance of the Property.
facts.F6: The 1st Defendant's solicitors informed those acting for the Plaintiff by a letter dated 11 February 1998 of the unilateral surrender by the tenant and that the Property would be conveyed with vacant possession to the Plaintiff.
facts.F7: The 1st Defendant transferred the Property to the 2nd Defendant and the Property has been re-let since around April 1998 for $72,500.00 per month rent.
facts.F8: The tenant under the tenancy had fallen into arrears on payment of rent and the Property was made subject of a Prohibition Order issued by the magistracy for illegal use for a restaurant business.
facts.F9: The landlord does not need to re-take possession of the property let in order to do any work on the property.
facts.F10: The 1st Defendant had taken possession of the Property through their solicitors' statement that the Property would be conveyed with vacant possession.
facts.F11: The tenant had unilaterally surrendered the lease.

reference_issues: Whether the 1st Defendant breached the agreement by re-taking possession of the Property.
Whether the Plaintiff is entitled to a reduction in price due to the 1st Defendant's alleged breach of the agreement.
Whether the 1st Defendant's conveyance of the Property with vacant possession is substantial performance.

Defendant: Nissho Iwai Hong Kong Corporation Limited and The Sanwa Bank Limited, Hong Kong Branch

facts.F1: The Plaintiff is an American company that entered into an agreement with Filon World Trade Company Limited for the supply of galvanized coil.
facts.F2: The method of payment to the Plaintiff was to be by letter of credit.
facts.F3: There were subsequent amendments to the Agreement in respect of the size and quantity of the goods.
facts.F4: The 2nd Defendant, Sanwa Bank, issued a letter of credit to the Plaintiff, with the 1st Defendant, Nissho Iwai, as the applicant.
facts.F5: Filon and Nissho Iwai entered into an agreement in which they agreed, among other things, that Nissho Iwai was to open the letter of credit in favour of the Plaintiff on Filon’s behalf.
facts.F6: The Plaintiff shipped the goods under the Agreement and presented the documents to Sanwa Bank, but there were discrepancies in the documents.
facts.F7: Sanwa Bank notified Corestates Bank of the discrepant documents and stated that it was 'Holding documents at your disposal pending instruction'.
facts.F8: The Plaintiff and the Defendants negotiated a solution, and Sanwa Bank agreed to pay 80% of the purchase price and the balance upon presentation of a draft survey report.
facts.F9: The Plaintiff presented the report, but Sanwa Bank refused to pay the balance, citing that the presentation of the report was outside the letter of credit.
facts.F10: The Notice of Refusal issued by Sanwa Bank was irreversible.
facts.F11: The letter of credit was at an end after the Notice of Refusal was issued.
facts.F12: Nissho Iwai had provided a promise to pay the Plaintiff as the applicant of the letter of credit and the Plaintiff had provided consideration for the promise to pay.
facts.F13: Sanwa Bank received the draft survey report, but refused to pay the balance.
facts.F14: The telex of 18th September 1995 did not connote any commitment or guarantee by Sanwa Bank to pay the Plaintiff.

reference_issues: Whether the words 'the balance amount in accordance with the above calculation will be paid on collection basis upon receipt of the above-mentioned Draft Survey Report' in Sanwa Bank's telex of 18th September 1995 would take Sanwa Bank's liability outside the letter of credit.
Whether the presentation of the report was outside the letter of credit.
Whether Nissho Iwai is liable for the balance of the purchase price as the applicant of the letter of credit.

facts.F1: The plaintiff was a director of the 1st defendant until he was summarily dismissed on 6 May 2008.
facts.F2: The 1st defendant is a wholly owned subsidiary of MF Jebsen International Limited (MFJIL), the principal company in a group of companies referred to for the purpose of this action as the MF Jebsen Group.
facts.F3: The plaintiff started working for YS Tso Limited as a marketing manager in 1996.
facts.F4: In 2001, the plaintiff was transferred to Datum Networks Corp Ltd (DNC) as general manager.
facts.F5: In about 2002, the JCL group underwent a restructuring.
facts.F6: The 2nd defendant relinquished his shares and directorships in JCL and formed the MF Jebsen Group.
facts.F7: The plaintiff was transferred to the 1st defendant in January 2007, taking up the post of managing director.
facts.F8: The 1st defendant's business did not fare well, and the plaintiff was unable to turn it around.
facts.F9: Concerns were raised about losses and expenditure incurred by the 1st defendant under the plaintiff's management.
facts.F10: A retrospective approval by the shareholders of the 1st defendant was sought for a personal loan from the 1st defendant to the plaintiff in the sum of AUD$735,803.39 (the AUD Loan).
facts.F11: This led to enquiries into other alleged wrongdoing, including purchases of school debentures, club debentures, etc., without written board approval.
facts.F12: After the plaintiff's dismissal, he claims that the defendants and the 2nd defendant in particular harassed him by repeated demands for repayment of the personal loan.
facts.F13: The defendants also allegedly defamed the plaintiff in front of others, notably Billy So, by leaving voicemail messages and in emails, and also in an email dated 9 May 2008 to Mr Billy Ma of the 1st defendant's solicitors.
facts.F14: The plaintiff had caused the 1st defendant to borrow from HSBC for his own purpose, without authorization from the board or the shareholders.
facts.F15: The plaintiff's relationship with the 1st defendant was not typical of normal business practice as it is commonly understood.

facts.F1: The Plaintiff was an employee of the Defendants on 19th January 1981 when he was engaged in work as an operator of a plastic injection moulding machine.
facts.F2: The Plaintiff was operating the machine, which was moulding parts for toy helicopters, and the movable mould platen opened but the item which had been moulded failed to drop off.
facts.F3: The Plaintiff reached into the machine to remove the piece of work when the platen suddenly and without warning closed on and crushed his left hand.
facts.F4: The injury resulted in the amputation of the Plaintiff's hand and part of his forearm.
facts.F5: The writ was issued out of the Supreme Court Registry on 28th October 1982, and its validity was extended for a period of one year under an order made by Master Hanson on 11th November 1983.
facts.F6: The second Defendant did not give notice of intention to defend, and interlocutory judgment was entered against him on 17th December 1982, with damages to be assessed and costs.
facts.F7: The first Defendant denied that the Plaintiff was employed by him at the time of the accident but did not provide evidence to support this claim.
facts.F8: The first Defendant was deemed to be the Plaintiff's employer at the time of the accident based on the evidence presented.
facts.F9: The Defendants did not attend the hearing, and the Court decided to proceed with the trial.
facts.F10: The Plaintiff was awarded damages for pain, suffering, and loss of amenities, loss of earnings from accident to trial, future loss of earnings, and special damages.
facts.F11: A certified copy of an application for registration of the business was presented as evidence.
facts.F12: The Plaintiff's testimony was presented as evidence.
facts.F13: Dr. Wedderburn's report recommended an impairment of 54% of the whole man for the Plaintiff's injury.
facts.F14: Published statistics on wage inflation were used to calculate the Plaintiff's average monthly rate of pay.
facts.F15: The Plaintiff's current rate of pay was used to select a multiplicand for future loss of earnings.

parties: Plaintiff: McKINSEY & COMPANY INC HONG KONG, MORGAN STANLEY ASIA LIMITED, SOLOMON BROTHERS, HONG KONG LIMITED
Defendant: SKY ALLIANCE DEVELOPMENT LIMITED

facts.F1: The applicants are seeking new tenancies for three houses in King's Court, 5 Mt. Kellett Road, the Peak.
facts.F2: The houses are three separate detached houses in a row of five, each having the same internal layout and area of about 350 m2, as well as the same view overlooking Aberdeen, the Lama Channel and the islands beyond.
facts.F3: The applicants for House A1 and House A2 are only disputing the new rent, while the tenant of House A3 is also seeking an additional clause in the new tenancy to permit the tenant to give 2 month's notice to terminate the tenancy after the expiration of 12 months.
facts.F4: The respondent is the owner of each of the houses and is opposed to the granting of the clause.
facts.F5: The respondent's valuer, Mr. Wu Kam Ming, valued House A1 at $127,000 per month exclusive of rates, House A2 at $125,000 per month exclusive of rates, and House A3 at $125,000 per month at the relevant dates.
facts.F6: The applicants' valuers, Mr. William Sham and Mr. Paul Brown, valued House A1 at $95,000 per month, House A2 at $95,000 per month, and House A3 at $91,000 per month.
facts.F7: The Tribunal inspected the houses and found that dampness was evident in each of them, but House A3 was not significantly worse than the others.
facts.F8: The landlord appeared to be taking steps to rectify the damp problem, which has been an ongoing issue since the houses were first let 2 years ago.
facts.F9: The Tribunal found that the applicant's proposed break clause does not seem to have affected the rent for House A2, and that such clauses are common in leases for premises at this level of the market.
facts.F10: The evidence of the valuers and the inspection of the houses showed that the damp problem is common to each of the houses.
facts.F11: The landlord is taking steps to rectify the damp problem.
facts.F12: The Tribunal has wider discretion to consider all relevant circumstances, including the fact that break clauses are common in leases for premises at this level of the market, when determining the terms of the new tenancy.
facts.F13: The applicant for House A3 failed to persuade the Tribunal that the occupant is likely to be transferred during the tenancy.
facts.F14: Comparable lettings in the area were used to determine the prevailing market rents for the houses.
facts.F15: The respondent's valuer did not provide conclusive evidence of the rental value of the houses.
facts.F16: The applicant's valuers provided more reliable comparable rents for the houses.

reference_issues: Whether the new rent for Houses A1, A2, and A3 should be adjusted for defects such as damp penetration.

facts.F9: The Former Trustees pursued the underlying application unreasonably and unjustifiably, despite being aware of the likelihood of failure.
facts.F10: The Former Trustees disregarded the Liquidators' statements and pursued the underlying summons unreasonably.
facts.F11: The Former Trustees were aware of the likelihood of failure of the underlying application.
facts.F12: The Former Trustees' conduct in the underlying application was unreasonable.

claim: Retrospective ratification of appointment of agents for liquidations and payment of fees and expenses
requested_remedy: Retrospective ratification of appointment of agents for liquidations and payment of fees and expenses
parties: Plaintiff: Official Receiver
Defendant: Various companies in liquidation (19 cases)

facts.F1: There were 19 applications by the Official Receiver seeking retrospective ratification of his appointment of agents for the purposes of the 19 liquidations.
facts.F2: Each of the liquidations in question was a summary liquidation conducted under the Panel B Scheme operated by the Official Receiver in the 1990s.
facts.F3: The Panel B Scheme involved outsourcing summary winding-up cases to private sector insolvency practitioners who were appointed by the Official Receiver to act as his agents in relation to the liquidations.
facts.F4: The Official Receiver's office did not have sufficient staff or resources to deal with the many more windings-up with which it was becoming burdened, leading to the launch of the Panel B Scheme.
facts.F5: 588 cases were appointed Panel B agents while the scheme was in place.
facts.F6: The terms of the appointment included undertakings signed by the partners of the firms of insolvency practitioners on Panel B and the initial terms of the pilot scheme.
facts.F7: The agents were required to report regularly to the Official Receiver and certain duties and acts remained entirely within the province of the Official Receiver's office.
facts.F8: Where assets were recovered, the agents would be remunerated out of the assets of the company in liquidation, subject to taxation by the court.
facts.F9: In cases where no assets were recovered or the assets recovered were insufficient to cover such remuneration, payment of the agent's fees (up to a limit of HK$60,000) was made out of a government subsidy.
facts.F10: The Official Receiver did not investigate the degree of delegation in each of the 19 cases due to proportionality and cost-effectiveness concerns.
facts.F11: The costs incurred in appointing the Panel B agents benefited the creditors and the liquidations generally.
facts.F12: No evidence of conflict of interest was presented and no complaints of improper or unsatisfactory conduct were made against the Official Receiver or the Panel B agents in any of the cases.

reference_issues: Whether the Official Receiver's appointment of agents for the purposes of the 19 liquidations was lawful and did not involve an impermissible delegation of his functions as liquidator.
Whether the court has power to ratify the appointment of the agents retrospectively under section 200(3) of the Companies Ordinance or its inherent jurisdiction.
Whether the exercise of such power would be in the interests of the creditors and the liquidations.
